blocks.text: Note in passing that a ventriloquist, as among the Greeks he was called Πύθων [Pythōn] and Εὐρυκλῆς [Eurykleēs], so among the Babylonians was called Σακχούρας [Sakchouras]. So Photius testifies, Author 94, from Iamblichus, On the Loves of Rhodanes and Sinonis: Καὶ ἐγγαστρίμυθον, ὃν καί φησιν, ὥσπερ Ἕλληνες μὲν Εὐρυκλέα λέγουσι, Βαβυλώνιοι δὲ Σακχούραν ἀποκαλοῦσι· [Kai engastrimython, hon kai phēsin, hōsper Hellēnes men Eurylea legousi, Babylōnioi de Sakchouran apokalousi]. Sacchuras is perhaps the Arabic ساحر [sāḥir] sachir, or سحار [saḥḥār] sacchar, which is what they call a magus. For magus, ساحر [sāḥir] sachir occurs in Actor. VIII, 9. and XIII, 8. and Deut. XVIII, 10., and the plural سحرة [saḥara] sachara in Act. XIX, 19. And from the singular سحار [saḥḥār] sacchar the plural سحارون [saḥḥārūn] saccharuna, Gen. XLI, 8. 24. And the feminine سحارة [saḥḥāra] sacchara for venefica [sorceress], Exod. XXII, 18. And سحر [siḥr] sichr for magia [magic] and veneficium [sorcery], Act. VIII, 9. and Galat. V, 20., in the Pentateuch and New Testament of the Erpenian edition. And the verb سحر [saḥara] sachara, or in the second conjugation sacchara, "to enchant", in the Nubian Geographer, Clim. 1, section 7: يسحرون الحيوان الضار [yasḥarūn al-ḥayawān al-ḍārr] They enchant harmful animals. Or, which seems to me more likely, sacchuras is זכורו zacchuru, or zechuru, as the Chaldeans and Syrians call a soothsayer, which is too well known to need proof. For examples see the Chaldee and Syriac paraphrases, Levit. XIX, 31. Deut. XVIII, 11. and 1 Sam. XXVIII, 3. etc. And in Sanhedrin fol. 65. 2. and 105. 1., and in Vajekra Rabba Sect. 26, etc. Thus from zacchuru would come sacchuras, with Z and S interchanged, as in Saguntum for Ζάκυνθος [Zakynthos] (for so Stephanus calls it), and in smaragdus for زمرجد [zumurjud] zmargiad.
